title: How to Build a Retirement Plan When You Have Multiple Income Sources
description: Coordinating Social Security, Pensions, Rentals, and Portfolio Withdrawals for tax efficiency.
content:
The traditional retirement model relies on a 'Three-Legged Stool': Social Security, Pensions, and Savings. Today, many retirees have a messy garage of income sources: a small pension from an old job, rental income from a duplex, Social Security, 401(k) RMDs, and maybe even a side hustle. Having multiple income streams is excellent for security, but it creates a tax complexity nightmare. If all these streams hit your bank account at once, they can push you into a high tax bracket and trigger Medicare surcharges. This guide explains how to layer and sequence your income.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Income Floor' Strategy: Categorize your income into 'Guaranteed' (Social Security/Pension) and 'Variable' (Portfolio/Rent). Use Guaranteed income to cover Fixed Expenses (Housing/Food). Use Variable income for Discretionary spending.
  • Tax Bracket Management: Fixed income sources (Pensions/RMDs) fill up the bottom of your tax bracket. You have less control over them. You must plan your flexible withdrawals (like IRA or Brokerage) around these fixed blocks to avoid spiking your tax rate.
  • Provisional Income Watch: Having too many income sources can make up to 85% of your Social Security taxable. Monitor your 'Combined Income' carefully.
  • The 'Fill the Gap' Method: Don't take portfolio withdrawals just because. Calculate your monthly spending need, subtract your fixed income sources, and withdraw only the difference. Reinvest the surplus.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US tax code taxes different income streams at different rates. Pension/401k = Ordinary Income. Social Security = 0-85% Taxable. Rental Income = Passive (offset by depreciation). Brokerage Sales = Capital Gains. Stacking these correctly is the key to keeping more money.

The Layered Income Cake

Visualize your income stacking up to fill tax buckets.

Layer 1: The Uncontrollables

These hit your tax return whether you want them to or not.

  • Social Security: $30,000/yr.
  • Pension: $20,000/yr.
  • RMDs (Age 73+): $40,000/yr.
  • Total Base Income: $90,000. (This already fills the 10% and 12% brackets).

Layer 2: The Flexibles

You need $120,000 to live. You need $30,000 more.

  • Option A: Withdraw from Traditional IRA. (Taxed at 22% marginal rate).
  • Option B: Withdraw from Roth IRA. (Taxed at 0%).
  • Option C: Sell Stocks in Brokerage. (Taxed at 15% Capital Gains).

The Strategy: Since your base income is already high ($90k), adding more Ordinary Income (Option A) hurts. Use Option B or C to top up your lifestyle without jumping tax brackets.

Optimization Tactics

  1. Roth Conversions Early: Before RMDs kick in (Age 73), your 'Uncontrollable' income is lower. Use the years 60-72 to convert IRA money to Roth. This lowers the RMD layer later.
  2. QLAC Strategy: If your RMDs are going to be too high, buy a Qualified Longevity Annuity Contract. You can move up to $200k out of the RMD calculation until age 85.
  3. Rental Depreciation: Use cost segregation or standard depreciation on rental properties to show a 'paper loss' or low income, even if cash flow is positive. This pairs well with high-tax pension income.
  4. Consolidate: Having 10 income sources is an administrative burden. Consider simplifying. Sell the rental property and buy a REIT. Roll old 401(k)s into one IRA.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I pay FICA taxes?

On pension/investment income? No. On side hustle income? Yes (15.3%). Factor this in if your 'multiple sources' includes active work.

What is IRMAA?

Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount. If your total income (MAGI) goes over ~$206k (couple), Medicare adds a surcharge to your premiums. Watch your total stack.

Should I reinvest dividends?

In retirement, usually No. Turn off DRIP. Let the dividends flow to cash. Use this cash to pay bills. It is the most passive income source you have.
